questions.q: According to this lesson, what does replication.factor actually control?
options: How many total copies of each partition Kafka keeps, spread across different brokers
How many consumers can read a topic at once
How many partitions a topic is split into
How long messages are retained before deletion
questions.explain: Replication factor is about durability — how many complete copies of a partition exist on different hardware.

questions.q: What is the difference between a partition's leader and its followers?
options: Only the leader serves reads and writes; followers just replicate from the leader to stay current
Followers serve all reads while the leader only handles writes
There is no difference — any replica can serve any request at any time
Followers store the data in a different format than the leader
questions.explain: All client traffic for a partition goes through its leader; followers exist purely to hold current, complete copies.

questions.q: What does min.insync.replicas=2 (with replication.factor=3) mean for a write, per this lesson?
options: The write must reach at least 2 replicas before being acknowledged; losing 2 of 3 brokers at once causes Kafka to refuse new writes
Exactly 2 replicas will always exist, no matter what replication.factor says
Only 2 consumers are allowed to read the topic at a time
The topic will delete itself if fewer than 2 replicas are in sync
questions.explain: min.insync.replicas is a durability floor — Kafka would rather stop accepting writes than acknowledge ones it can't guarantee survive.

questions.q: In this lesson's leader-failure sequence, what happens immediately after the controller notices the leader broker is unresponsive?
options: A new leader is elected from the in-sync replica (ISR) set, with zero data loss
The entire topic is deleted and recreated
All producers and consumers must be manually reconfigured
The cluster waits indefinitely for the original leader to come back before doing anything
questions.explain: An ISR member already has everything the old leader had, so promoting it loses nothing.

questions.q: Why is a follower that has fallen behind temporarily removed from the ISR set?
options: Because it isn't fully caught up to the leader, so it isn't yet a safe candidate to be promoted without losing data
Because Kafka deletes any replica that ever falls behind, permanently
Because only in-sync replicas are allowed to receive new writes from producers directly
ISR membership has nothing to do with catch-up status
questions.explain: ISR membership specifically tracks which replicas are safe to promote to leader without losing acknowledged data.
